tagline: Prince Hall Grand Master and voting rights organizer who gave Atlanta's "Sweet Auburn" its name
burial: Buried at South-View Cemetery, as reported by CBS News Atlanta, which lists him among the civic leaders buried there; a Patch article reportedly also lists his grave site. No official South-View burial record or plot location was found in the research.

sections.heading: Early life and family
sections.text: John Wesley Dobbs was born in 1882 in Marietta, Georgia, to Minnie and Will Dobbs, who separated when he was about two years old. In 1906 John Wesley Dobbs married Irene Ophelia Thompson. The couple had six daughters, and all six graduated from Spelman College. Their fifth daughter, Mattiwilda Dobbs, became an internationally known opera singer. His grandson Maynard Jackson became Atlanta's first Black mayor. According to the King Papers at Stanford, the family of Martin Luther King Sr. moved to Boulevard near the Dobbs home in 1941, and the children of the two families played together.

sections.heading: Education
sections.text: John Wesley Dobbs began attending school full time in Savannah, Georgia, in 1891. In 1897 he enrolled at Atlanta Baptist College, the school that later became Morehouse College, but he left to care for his ill mother. John Wesley Dobbs never earned a college degree. According to the New Georgia Encyclopedia, he kept studying on his own, educating himself while he built a long career in the postal service and in civic life.

sections.heading: Career and achievements
sections.text: John Wesley Dobbs passed the civil service exam in 1903 and became a railway mail clerk for the U.S. Post Office in Atlanta, a job he held for 32 years. By 1949 the New Georgia Encyclopedia describes him as a retired postal employee. Dobbs was initiated into the Prince Hall Masons in 1911 and was elected Grand Master of the Prince Hall Masons of Georgia in 1932. The King Papers give his tenure as Grand Master as 1932 to 1961, the year of his death. His election as Grand Master earned John Wesley Dobbs his lasting nickname, "the Grand." His Masonic leadership gave him a statewide platform that he used for civic and political organizing in Black Atlanta.

sections.heading: Civil rights and civic life
sections.text: John Wesley Dobbs founded the Atlanta Civic and Political League in 1936 and worked toward registering 10,000 Black voters in Atlanta. He helped win the hiring of eight Black police officers in 1948, though they were limited to patrolling Black neighborhoods, and in 1949 he helped win street lamps for Auburn Avenue. On July 7, 1949, the Atlanta Negro Voters League was founded at the Butler Street YMCA as a bipartisan group; Dobbs, a Republican who led the Fulton County Republican Club, served as one of its first co-chairs alongside A. T. Walden. The league ran voter registration committees, screened candidates, published slates in the Atlanta Daily World, announced them on WERD, offered rides to the polls, and backed Mayor William B. Hartsfield in 1949, 1953 and 1957. In 1953 John Wesley Dobbs split with the league because no Black firemen had been hired, withdrawing his Republican supporters; Rev. William Jackson replaced him in 1954. Dobbs coined the name "Sweet Auburn" for the Auburn Avenue district and was called the "unofficial mayor of Auburn Avenue."

sections.heading: Legacy and honors
sections.text: John Wesley Dobbs suffered a stroke on August 21, 1961, and died nine days later, on August 30, 1961, at age 79. His funeral was held on September 2, 1961, at Big Bethel AME Church in Atlanta. Martin Luther King Jr. gave the invocation, William Holmes Borders of Wheat Street Baptist Church gave the eulogy, and Thurgood Marshall served as a pallbearer. John Wesley Dobbs was buried at South-View Cemetery. On January 10, 1994, his grandson, Mayor Maynard Jackson, renamed Atlanta's Houston Street as John Wesley Dobbs Avenue in his honor.

sections.heading: Did you know?
sections.text: John Wesley Dobbs is the man who gave Auburn Avenue the name "Sweet Auburn." He was the grandfather of Maynard Jackson, Atlanta's first Black mayor, who in 1994 renamed Houston Street as John Wesley Dobbs Avenue in his honor. Martin Luther King Jr. gave the invocation at his 1961 funeral, and Thurgood Marshall was one of his pallbearers. All six of his daughters graduated from Spelman College, including the opera singer Mattiwilda Dobbs.

sections.heading: Where sources disagree
sections.text: Sources disagree on when John Wesley Dobbs co-founded the Atlanta Negro Voters League with A. T. Walden. The New Georgia Encyclopedia's biography of Dobbs gives 1946, while the New Georgia Encyclopedia's own article on the league gives a founding date of July 7, 1949, at the Butler Street YMCA. The Atlanta History Center reportedly also supports 1949. This profile uses 1949 as the better-supported date. The 1946 date may be a confusion with the 1946 federal ruling that struck down Georgia's white primary, which the league article mentions. Sources also describe his voter registration work differently: the New Georgia Encyclopedia says he worked toward registering 10,000 Black voters in Atlanta, while CBS News Atlanta credits him with registering over 10,000 African Americans in Georgia.

tagline: Atlanta-born soprano, first African American to sing a lead role at La Scala, who refused segregated stages
burial: Her South-View burial is weakly sourced: she is listed in the South-View book by Henderson (2018) as buried there, and a Toni Morrison Society page (seen only as a search summary) reportedly lists her among those interred at South-View, but no obituary, funeral notice, plot location or burial date confirming it was found.

sections.heading: Early life and family
sections.text: Mattiwilda Dobbs was born on July 11, 1925, in Atlanta, the fifth of six daughters of John Wesley Dobbs and Irene Ophelia Thompson. She was named for her maternal grandmother, Mattie Wilda Sykes. Her nephew Maynard Jackson became Atlanta's first Black mayor, and her sister June Dobbs Butts survived her. Mattiwilda Dobbs married Luis Rodriguez, who died of a liver ailment in June 1954, about 14 months after their wedding. Just before Christmas 1957 she married the Swedish newspaperman Bengt Janzon in New York, and she was later known as Mattiwilda Dobbs Janzon. Bengt Janzon died in 1997.

sections.heading: Education
sections.text: Mattiwilda Dobbs earned a music degree from Spelman College in 1946 and graduated as class valedictorian. She went on to study voice in New York with Lotte Leonard. Mattiwilda Dobbs won a Marian Anderson Award and a John Hay Whitney Fellowship, and the fellowship funded her further study in Europe, which led to her international career. Decades later, in 1979, Spelman College awarded Mattiwilda Dobbs an honorary doctorate.

sections.heading: Career and achievements
sections.text: Mattiwilda Dobbs, a coloratura soprano, won the International Music Competition in Geneva, Switzerland, in 1951. In 1953 she sang Elvira in Rossini's L'italiana in Algeri at La Scala in Milan, becoming the first African American to sing a lead role there. Her U.S. debut came in New York in 1954. In 1956 she made her Metropolitan Opera debut as Gilda in Verdi's Rigoletto. Mattiwilda Dobbs was the first Black woman offered a long-term contract by the Met, where she sang 29 performances in six roles over eight seasons. In 1974 she began teaching at the University of Texas, the first African American artist on its faculty, and she was Spelman's artist-in-residence in 1974-75. She later became a professor of voice at Howard University. Mattiwilda Dobbs gave recitals until at least 1990 and served on the Metropolitan Opera board and the National Endowment for the Arts Solo Recital Panel.

sections.heading: Civil rights and civic life
sections.text: Mattiwilda Dobbs refused to perform for segregated audiences, following the example of Paul Robeson. According to a Philadelphia Inquirer obituary (seen as a search summary), this meant she did not sing professionally in her hometown of Atlanta until 1962. That year, after the Atlanta Municipal Auditorium was desegregated, Mattiwilda Dobbs sang there before a large integrated audience. Mayor Ivan Allen Jr. joined her onstage and presented her with a key to the city.

sections.heading: Legacy and honors
sections.text: Mattiwilda Dobbs is remembered as a pioneer: the first African American to sing a lead role at La Scala, in 1953, and the first Black woman given a long-term contract by the Metropolitan Opera. Her honors included the 1951 Geneva International Music Competition prize, a Marian Anderson Award, a John Hay Whitney Fellowship, a key to the city of Atlanta in 1962, and an honorary doctorate from Spelman College in 1979. Mattiwilda Dobbs died on December 8, 2015, at her home in Atlanta, after what the Atlanta Journal-Constitution called a brief bout with cancer. She was 90.

sections.heading: Did you know?
sections.text: Mattiwilda Dobbs was the first African American to sing a lead role at La Scala, as Elvira in 1953. She would not sing for segregated audiences, so her 1962 Atlanta homecoming concert was before an integrated audience, and the mayor gave her a key to the city. She was the first Black woman given a long-term Metropolitan Opera contract, debuting as Gilda in 1956. Mattiwilda Dobbs was the daughter of John Wesley Dobbs and the aunt of Mayor Maynard Jackson.

sections.heading: Where sources disagree
sections.text: Sources differ slightly on two points about Mattiwilda Dobbs. On her place of death, the New Georgia Encyclopedia and the League of American Orchestras obituary say she died at her Atlanta home, while a Philadelphia Inquirer obituary (seen only as a search summary) reportedly says a retirement community in Atlanta. This profile uses her home, the better-supported account. On her 1954 U.S. debut in New York, the New Georgia Encyclopedia describes it as a recital, while the League of American Orchestras says she appeared with the Little Orchestra Society; both place it in New York in 1954.

tagline: Hall of Famer who broke Babe Ruth's home run record in Atlanta in 1974 and finished with 755 home runs
burial: Buried at South-View Cemetery on January 27, 2021, after his funeral at Friendship Baptist Church, as reported by the Associated Press, which calls South-View "the oldest Black burial ground in Atlanta."

sections.heading: Early life and family
sections.text: Henry Louis "Hank" Aaron was born on February 5, 1934, in Mobile, Alabama, the third of eight children of Estella and Herbert Aaron. Hank Aaron was married to Billye Aaron, who survived him. His children were Gaile, Hank Jr., Lary, Dorinda and Ceci, and he was also survived by grandchildren. According to the New Georgia Encyclopedia, his daughter Gaile attended Fisk University. Hank Aaron died in Atlanta in 2021.

sections.heading: Education
sections.text: Hank Aaron grew up in Mobile, Alabama, where he was born in 1934. According to the New Georgia Encyclopedia, Henry Louis Aaron attended two schools in Mobile: Central High School and the Josephine Allen Institute. In the spring of 1952, at age 18, Hank Aaron joined the Indianapolis Clowns of the Negro Leagues as a shortstop, beginning the professional baseball career that made him famous.

sections.heading: Career and achievements
sections.text: Hank Aaron joined the Negro Leagues' Indianapolis Clowns in spring 1952 at age 18 and led the league with a .467 average. In 1953 he was MVP of the minor-league Sally League. The Boston Braves bought his contract, and he debuted in the majors in 1954, playing for the Milwaukee Braves (1954-1965), the Atlanta Braves (1966-1974) and the Milwaukee Brewers (1975-1976). In 1957 Aaron was National League MVP (.322, 44 home runs, 132 RBI) and won the World Series. He won three Gold Gloves and was selected to 25 All-Star games. On May 17, 1970, he became the first player with both 3,000 hits and 500 home runs. On April 8, 1974, at Atlanta-Fulton County Stadium, Hank Aaron hit No. 715 off the Dodgers' Al Downing, passing Babe Ruth. He retired as a player in 1976 with 755 home runs, a record 2,297 RBI, 3,771 hits, a record 6,856 total bases, a .305 average, 3,298 games, 2,174 runs and 1,477 extra-base hits, the most in MLB history. He was inducted into the Hall of Fame in 1982, his first year of eligibility. Aaron then worked in the Braves front office, reportedly as senior vice president from December 1989, and held posts with Turner Broadcasting.

sections.heading: Civil rights and civic life
sections.text: Hank Aaron's public role extended beyond baseball. Speaking at Aaron's funeral, former President Bill Clinton said that Aaron's 1992 endorsement had helped him carry Georgia. In 2010 Hank Aaron was inducted as a Georgia Trustee. In 1991 he published his autobiography, I Had a Hammer, written with Lonnie Wheeler. After his death, his family asked that, in lieu of flowers, donations be made to the Chasing the Dream Foundation in Atlanta.

sections.heading: Legacy and honors
sections.text: Hank Aaron was inducted into the Baseball Hall of Fame in 1982 and received the Presidential Medal of Freedom from President George W. Bush in 2002. His career home run record stood until Barry Bonds broke it in August 2007, and he still holds MLB records for RBI and total bases. Atlanta has a Hank Aaron Drive, and a display marks where No. 715 landed at the former Atlanta-Fulton County Stadium site; the stadium was imploded in 1997. Muhammad Ali called him "the only man I idolize more than myself." Hank Aaron died in Atlanta on January 22, 2021, of natural causes at 86. The Braves held a memorial at Truist Park, and his funeral on January 27 at Friendship Baptist Church, limited to about 50 people by COVID-19 rules, featured Bill Clinton, Bud Selig and Andrew Young, plus a video message from Jimmy Carter. The hearse passed the site of No. 715 and Hank Aaron Drive on the way to South-View Cemetery, also the resting place of John Lewis and Julian Bond.

sections.heading: Did you know?
sections.text: Hank Aaron's funeral procession detoured past the spot where he hit home run No. 715 on its way to South-View Cemetery. He still holds Major League Baseball records for runs batted in (2,297) and total bases (6,856). Even without his 755 home runs, Hank Aaron would still have 3,016 hits. He began his professional career in the Negro Leagues with the Indianapolis Clowns in 1952. Bill Clinton spoke at his funeral and said Aaron's 1992 endorsement helped him carry Georgia.

sections.heading: Where sources disagree
sections.text: Sources disagree on how many times Hank Aaron was an All-Star. The Baseball Hall of Fame and the New Georgia Encyclopedia both say he had 25 All-Star selections, while the Atlanta Journal-Constitution obituary calls him a "20-time All-Star." This profile uses 25, the figure given by the two more authoritative sources. Sources also differ in detail on his front-office career: an AP report (seen as a search summary) says he worked for the Braves from 1976 and was senior vice president from December 1989, while the New Georgia Encyclopedia says only that he held several posts with the Braves and Turner Broadcasting.
